sentences.text: The type specimen of Talenkauen is a partial articulated skeleton missing the rear skull, tail, and hands.
The estimated body length of Talenkauen is no more than 4 meters.
Talenkauen retained premaxillary teeth at the tip of its beak and a first toe, features lost in more derived iguanodontians.
Talenkauen is notable for smooth, ovoid plates located along the sides of its rib cage.
The rib plates of Talenkauen could be up to 180 millimeters long but were only 3 millimeters thick.
Wear on the 1.7mm wide teeth of a neonatal Talenkauen fossil indicates the baby had hatched and fed shortly before dying.
The holotype specimen of Talenkauen was collected in February 2000 and formally named in 2004 by Fernando E. Novas and colleagues.
Talenkauen was discovered on Los Hornos Hill near the coast of Viedma Lake in Santa Cruz Province, Argentina.
An extensive description of Talenkauen was published in 2020 by Sebastián Rozadilla and colleagues.
As a basal ornithopod, Talenkauen was likely a small, bipedal herbivore.
Researchers suggested Talenkauen's rib plates might function like uncinate processes found in birds and crocodiles to help ventilate lungs.
Talenkauen belongs to the parent group Elasmaria.
Talenkauen is classified within the class Ornithischia.
Talenkauen lived during the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous.
Fossils of Talenkauen have been found in the Austral Basin of Santa Cruz, Argentina.
Talenkauen lived during the Campanian stage, between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
